The Chadian government has confirmed that its territory was attacked by Sudan after the Sudanese Air Force bombed a logistics convoy belonging to the UAE-backed Rapid Support Forces (RSF), 100 km inside Chadian territory.
Interestingly, Chad continues to deny any involvement in the war, despite repeated evidence of logistics convoys crossing from its territory into RSF-controlled areas.

The U.S. Navy has unveiled its new AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile (LRAAM), also known as Malice. The missile is currently undergoing flight testing and is intended for deployment on the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, F-35C, and the future F/A-XX fighter.
Images released by the Navy show the missile mounted on a Super Hornet, as well as carried internally in the F-35C’s weapons bay.
The missile is a two-stage design developed by Raytheon. It is said to be more than 4 meters long, weigh approximately 680 kg, and have a stated range of over 460 km.

The Chief of Staff of Iran’s Armed Forces, Major General Ali Abdollahi, visited one of Iran’s underground facilities involved in the production of ballistic missiles.
The visit is a clear message to those claiming that Iran is no longer capable of producing ballistic missiles, particularly solid-fuel systems. What has been destroyed on the surface is nothing compared to what remains underground.
I spoke with several people from Iranian military circles, and they confirmed to me that pre-war munitions are still stockpiled in quantities sufficient to last for years. This means reports based on “intelligence” estimates of Iran’s remaining ballistic missile inventory should be taken with caution, as they are often based on very limited information. Thousands upon thousands of ballistic missiles are still stockpiled.
On top of that, production has increased significantly, while upgrades are constantly being made to improve the accuracy and overall performance of the missiles.
As for the drones, one person put it simply: “We have drones that can go for centuries.”
That doesn’t mean everything is fine or that Iran has no problems. There are shortages of trained ballistic missile operators, and recruitment has already started. The reason is obvious: not everyone can be selected to join the IRGC Aerospace Force, as there are specific criteria that candidates have to meet.

U.S. State Department approved a $2.3 billion Foreign Military Sale (FMS) to Norway for 21 UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters.
The package includes 46 T700-GE-701D engines, 25 AN/AAR-57 Common Missile Warning Systems, 25 Common Infrared Countermeasure systems, 25 AN/APR-39E(V)2 radar warning receivers, 50 EAGLE-M+429 embedded GPS/inertial navigation systems, 100 AN/ARC-231A radios and 18 M240H machine guns.

Huge anti-drone structures have been erected over oil storage tanks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, following strikes by Iranian Shahed-136 loitering munitions.
These structures can help mitigate the damage, but they do not provide 100% protection. On the other hand, missiles will get the job done.

The Israeli Air Force (IAF) has received its second Boeing KC-46A Pegasus aerial refueling aircraft at Nevatim Air Base.
The KC-46A tankers will initially be operated by the newly established 46th Squadron. In the future, the squadron is expected to be incorporated into the IAF’s 120th “Desert Giants” Squadron.

The UK Ministry of Defence says development of the future Stratus cruise and anti-ship missile is nearing the demonstration phase, with full-scale testing planned for 2028.
Development of the missile’s airframe, engine, warhead, and guidance system has reportedly been completed. It is expected to be integrated with Typhoon and Rafale fighters, as well as naval platforms such as Type 26 frigates.
The MoD declined to disclose the missile’s range, stating only that it will exceed the Storm Shadow’s 560 km range and the Harpoon’s 220 km range.

Denmark and Italy push forward on migration control.
The EU Parliament has voted to back new rules for return hubs outside Europe. This allows faster returns of rejected asylum seekers and irregular migrants to third countries, speeding up deportations and strengthening border management.
Led by efforts from Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, Europe is moving toward more pragmatic, effective migration policies.
